roblox-dev.name: Roblox Development & Game Design
videos: Popularity is designed, not lucky: pick a proven genre, make the first minutes clear and rewarding, and plan updates before launch.
Games that blow up pair a simple, instantly-readable hook with retention and shareable moments; the algorithm amplifies stats, not effort.
Realistic dev journey: most first games flop; ship small, learn from data, and treat each release as practice for the next.
Study top games in your genre before building: copy the proven structure (loop, UI, progression), differentiate on theme.
Viral games are usually simple ideas executed fast with a strong thumbnail/title; scope small and iterate.
Postmortem of a 30-day front-page game: tight scope, quick launch, ads to seed data, then rapid updates driven by stats.
Growth do's/don'ts: update consistently, fix stats one at a time, don't clickbait thumbnails, don't over-monetize early.
Costly mistakes: overscoping, launching without analytics, ignoring mobile, spending ads on an unfixed game, weak thumbnails.
Long-form primer on what to know before building: genre choice, scope, the stats the algorithm reads, and planning monetization from day one.
Trying to make 'the best game ever' first produced an unfocused mess; small, focused scope beats ambition on a first game.
Repeatable process (not luck): validate idea, build core loop fast, launch with ads, iterate on retention/playtime.
Devs quit from burnout and unrealistic expectations; ship many small games and treat failures as data.
Viral game case study: strong hook + polished thumbnails/icon/UI art; presentation quality drives click-through.
Comedic but accurate stages of Roblox dev (idea hype, scope creep, bugs, launch reality); plan for the unglamorous middle.
A viral game died because it lacked depth/updates; the sequel focused on longer-term progression and content cadence.
The '80/20 formula': ~80% proven mechanics players already understand, ~20% fresh twist/theme.
Common dev mistakes: no prototyping, polishing before fun is proven, building systems nobody uses, not playtesting with strangers.
Advertise correctly: test many thumbnails, small steady sponsor budgets, judge after several days, and fix the game before scaling spend.
Use Roblox Funnel analytics: log each onboarding/core-loop step, find the biggest drop-off, fix that single step, repeat.
Fun comes from clear goals + constant feedback + meaningful progress; test the core action in isolation before adding systems.
patterns: **Scope small, ship fast, iterate on data.** Nearly every success story is a tightly-scoped game launched in days/weeks, then improved weekly using stats.
**80% proven / 20% novel.** Reuse genre conventions players already understand (loops, UI layout, progression); spend novelty on theme and one twist.
**Stats drive the algorithm.** Session length, D1/D7 retention, play-through rate and monetization are what Home recommendations reward; effort or graphics alone don't.
**Packaging is half the game.** Thumbnails, icon and title determine whether anyone tries the game; test many variants.
**First games fail; that's the curriculum.** Creators frame flops as practice and recommend many small releases over one giant project.
**Instrument from day one.** Funnels on onboarding and the core loop are the fastest way to find what's broken.

retention.name: Player Retention
videos: Ethical engagement: keep players through intrinsic motivation (mastery, curiosity, autonomy) instead of compulsion tricks; respect players' time and let them stop.
Players will optimize the fun out of a game; designers must shape incentives so the optimal strategy is also the fun one.
Official explainer of D1/D7/D30 retention on the Creator Dashboard and why it's a key quality signal for recommendations.
Official onboarding techniques: get to the fun quickly, teach by doing, use contextual hints, and give an early win.
Roblox's onboarding essentials: fast early levels, starter items/currency, visible short/mid/long goals, a designed 'moment of joy', funnel each step.
Bee Swarm Simulator's creator on FTUE: intrigue new players with an inviting world and immediate progress, then reveal depth gradually.
Read your stats as a diagnosis: low playtime = weak loop, low D1 = weak FTUE/hook, low D7 = weak progression; fix the weakest first.
Mobile retention: short sessions with clear goals, daily reasons to return, progression that's always visible.
Returning after a break is hard (forgotten controls/goals); 'welcome back' recaps and gentle re-onboarding reduce lapsed-player churn.
Path of Exile keeps players returning with regular content leagues (fresh starts), deep build mastery, and fair monetization.
GDC: move retention design from rational hooks (rewards) to emotional ones (attachment, identity, social belonging).
GDC: time-based systems (timers, energy, daily cycles) structure F2P sessions; use them to create appointments, not walls.
GDC: narrative and character attachment give players emotional reasons to come back beyond rewards.
Study of 1,460 app onboarding flows: fewer steps, value shown before asks, progressive disclosure, personalization.
Four kinds of exploration (spatial, mechanical, narrative, social) each create curiosity; layered secrets reward continued play.
Catalogue of compulsion techniques (variable rewards, loss aversion, sunk cost) - useful as a list of dark patterns to avoid or use carefully.
Tutorials should feel like play: teach inside the real game with natural prompts, not walls of text.
Be kind to beginners: lower early difficulty, give generous early wins, let experts skip ahead.
Small-game growth: tighten the first session, update often, and use stats (not gut feeling) to pick what to fix next.
Recent algorithm changes weight long-term behavior (retention, returning players, friend invites) over launch-day spikes.
patterns: **Fun in the first minute, payoff within five.** Every source stresses an immediate first action, an early win, and a visible next goal; Roblox's own guidance targets reaching the fun within ~5 minutes.
**Teach by doing.** Short contextual prompts (arrows, beams, highlights) beat text tutorials; funnel every tutorial step and fix the worst one.
**Give a concrete reason to return tomorrow.** Something growing/finishing while away, an escalating daily reward, a friend's progress - tied to the real goal, not just free currency.
**D1 = onboarding, D7 = progression, D30 = content and social.** Diagnose retention by phase instead of adding daily rewards everywhere.
**Emotional > rational hooks.** Attachment (pets, bases, identity), mastery and social belonging hold players longer than reward schedules alone.
**Avoid compulsion traps.** Loss aversion, sunk-cost pressure and punishing absence raise short-term numbers but damage trust; respect stopping points.

gameplay-loops.name: Gameplay Loops
videos: Loops nest: moment-to-moment action, a session loop of goals, and a long-term loop of progression; each layer must be satisfying on its own.
Design a loop as action → reward → upgrade → harder/better action, and make sure each step is clear to the player.
Good progression unlocks new ways to play (variety, options), not just bigger numbers; pure stat treadmills feel like Skinner boxes.
Timothy Cain (Fallout co-creator): define the core loop early, keep it simple, and test that the repeated action is enjoyable before content.
Explains loop terminology (core, meta, feedback loops) with examples; useful vocabulary for designing and documenting loops.
Game economies need balanced faucets (sources) and drains (sinks); unchecked inflation trivializes rewards.
Progression systems should give players choices and expression; the anticipation of the next unlock is itself the reward.
'Chains' instead of loops: think of play as a sequence of goals that evolve and lead somewhere, not a circle that repeats unchanged.
A good level-up system gives noticeable, felt power gains and meaningful choices at each level; invisible +1% upgrades don't motivate.
The real core loop every game shares: the player forms a goal, acts, gets feedback, and learns; design for that learning cycle.
Positive feedback loops snowball (winner gets stronger); negative loops (catch-up) keep things competitive; use them deliberately.
Lecture contrasting healthy core loops with compulsion loops (reward-anticipation cycles); know which one you're building.
GDC: idle/incremental games run on exponential growth, prestige/reset loops and offline progress; monetize speed and automation.
Good incrementals keep introducing new mechanics/layers as numbers grow, so the game changes, not just the digits.
Catalogue of creative progression mechanics (unlocks that change how you play) as alternatives to plain stat increases.
Permanent (meta) progression mechanics that carry across runs/resets, keeping repeat play meaningful.
Stardew Valley: daily short-term goals feed seasonal/long-term goals; every session ends with progress made.
Tycoon devlog: add side loops (mini-activities, collectibles, quests) around the main income loop to add variety and session time.
Building a Roblox simulator in 7 days: click/collect → sell → upgrade → new zone; rebirths reset for multipliers.
Turn an idea into gameplay by writing its loop first: what the player does repeatedly, why, and what changes over time.
patterns: **Three nested loops.** Moment-to-moment action (seconds) → session goals (minutes) → long-term progression (days); each layer needs its own payoff.
**Write the loop as a sentence:** action → feedback/reward → progression choice → more expressive or harder action. If you can't, the design isn't clear yet.
**Progression must change play, not just numbers.** New zones, tools, mechanics and abilities beat +X% stat treadmills.
**Economies need sinks.** Every currency source needs a matching drain (upgrades, rebirths, cosmetics) or inflation kills reward value.
**Prestige/rebirth loops** let simulator/incremental games extend content cheaply: reset progress for a permanent multiplier and a new layer.
**Prove the core action is fun first.** Prototype the repeated action in isolation before building content or meta systems.

ui-design.name: UI Design
videos: Fast UI upgrades: consistent palette, rounded corners, strokes, gradients, drop shadows and clear hierarchy make Roblox UI look professional.
Good UI is mostly discipline: consistent spacing, alignment, readable fonts and a limited palette; laziness, not talent, is the gap.
Modern pro Roblox UI is built with React-Luau (component-based, state-driven) for maintainability in larger games.
Design cartoony Roblox UI in Figma first (thick outlines, bold colors, chunky buttons), then import to Studio.
Stud-style UI (Roblox-native chunky 3D look) workflow in Figma; matches the visual language many top games use.
Beginner GUI fundamentals: ScreenGui, Frames, Scale vs Offset, layouts (UIListLayout/UIGridLayout), anchoring.
Improve existing UI step by step: reduce clutter, add icons, use consistent button styles, improve contrast.
Scale UI across phones, tablets and PC: use Scale sizing, UIAspectRatioConstraint, anchor points, and test on device emulators.
Smooth button feedback with TweenService: hover/press scale, color shift, and sound make buttons feel responsive.
Animate UI (open/close transitions, hover states, bounces) so the interface feels alive and responsive.
Add effects to UI (gradients animating, shine sweeps, particles) to draw attention to important buttons like the shop.
UI design basics for Roblox: hierarchy, contrast, consistency, and leaving breathing room.
Critique of modern game UIs: cluttered HUDs, menus nested too deep, and style over readability hurt the experience.
Fonts carry tone and readability; pick a font that fits the game's mood and stays legible at small sizes.
Color psychology: use color consistently to signal meaning (rarity, danger, reward) and set emotional tone.
Diegetic (in-world) UI can increase immersion but must stay readable; mix diegetic and screen UI pragmatically.
Examples of games with great UI: strong style identity, clarity under pressure, and smooth navigation.
Mobile game UI workflow: big thumb-friendly buttons, bright readable icons, and layouts designed for the screen edges.
Designing a battle/season pass screen: clear tier track, free vs premium rows, and previewed rewards.
Animated shop GUI in Roblox: open animation, item cards, and purchase buttons that feel rewarding.
patterns: **Mobile-first sizing.** Most Roblox players are on phones: Scale-based layouts, aspect-ratio constraints, safe areas, and thumb-sized buttons (≥ ~44px).
**Consistency beats decoration.** One palette, one button style, consistent spacing and icons do more than individual flashy elements.
**Every button reacts.** Hover/press tweens + a click sound are the cheapest polish with the biggest feel improvement.
**Design in Figma, build in Studio.** Pros mock up screens first, then import; stud/cartoony styles fit Roblox's visual language.
**Color and type carry meaning.** Use color to encode rarity/reward/danger and keep fonts legible at small sizes.
**Minimal HUD, clear hierarchy.** Show only what matters now; surface the shop and next goal clearly without clutter.

monetization.name: Monetization
videos: Official RDC 2026 session with top creators' monetization lessons; layered products (passes, dev products, subscriptions) tied to gameplay value.
The two easiest ways the creator found to earn Robux on Roblox, framed against low-effort tutorials; focus on proven product types.
Breakdown of a 38K-CCU game's strategy and products; revenue comes from retention and many purchase pathways, not one product.
A 100-CCU game earned ~2M Robux: game passes and dev products that sold, and why retention/monetization depth beats raw CCU.
Small developer's year earning 23M Robux across games: many smaller titles, data-driven iteration, and focused products.
Monetization basics: game passes (one-time perks), developer products (repeatable), Premium payouts, and how to price them.
Top monetization methods for Roblox games: passes, dev products, VIP/private servers, cosmetics, and limited-time offers.
Which developer products sold most in a $43K game and why: products that solve a pain at the moment players feel it.
How to add monetization to your game: placement of shop/purchase prompts and the types of items that sell.
Eight psychological 'traps' behind Roblox spending (scarcity, anchoring, sunk cost...) - know them to use ethically or avoid.
Scripting developer products correctly: ProcessReceipt, idempotent server-side granting, saving purchases.
Selling developer products with ProfileStore so purchases are granted once and persist safely.
F2P 'whale' monetization tricks explained; a cautionary look at manipulative designs and their reputational cost.
Day with Roblox millionaire devs: teams treat games as businesses - data, updates, ads, and monetization tuning.
Real earnings of a 2k+ CCU game; shows revenue per CCU varies hugely with monetization design.
Realistic earnings ranges for Roblox games and what separates well- from poorly-monetized games.
How much Roblox developers actually make: a few hits earn most; most games earn little - plan for many attempts.
DevEx walkthrough: converting earned Robux to real money, rates and requirements.
Story of a game earning ~14M Robux in one week; how a viral spike plus ready monetization captured revenue.
Small-scale reality check: three games, $130 of ads, ~9k visits - read straight from the dashboard.
patterns: **Sell pain-relievers and expression, not walls.** Best sellers remove friction (speed, auto-collect, protection, offline gains) or let players show off (cosmetics, rare items).
**Layer products.** Combine one-time game passes, repeatable developer products, and optional subscriptions/VIP servers at several price points.
**Consumables build habits.** Cheap repeatable products (boosts, refills) raise spending frequency more than one-off passes.
**Placement and timing matter.** Put offers where players are and when they feel the need (e.g. 'not enough coins' → shop), not as interrupting popups.
**Revenue per CCU varies 10-30x.** Monetization depth and retention, not player count, decide earnings.
**Server-authoritative, idempotent purchases.** Grant in ProcessReceipt on the server and persist safely - lost purchases destroy trust.
**No pay-to-win or manipulative pressure.** Creators and the critical videos agree: it kills retention and reputation.

fun.name: What Makes a Game Fun (feel, pacing, risk/reward, novelty, social)
videos: Game feel = responsive controls + layered feedback (animation, particles, sound, screen shake, hit-pause); tune it until actions feel good on their own.
'Juice it or lose it': the same game transformed by tweening, squash/stretch, particles, sound and shake - juice multiplies satisfaction cheaply.
Vlambeer's ~30 feel tricks: screen shake, hit-stop, big bullets/impacts, recoil/knockback, permanence (debris stays), sound punch.
Even a single button press becomes fun with anticipation, squash, particles, sound and reaction - feedback design matters more than content.
Quick wins for fun: tighten feedback, add variety and surprise, reduce downtime and frustration.
Ten concrete game-feel improvements: input buffering, coyote time, easing, camera work, impact frames, audio layering.
Input randomness (before the player acts) creates interesting decisions; output randomness (after) can feel unfair - choose deliberately.
Overjustification effect: heavy extrinsic rewards can make an intrinsically fun activity feel like a chore.
Think like a designer: start from the experience/feeling you want, then design mechanics that produce it.
Sakurai: risk and reward should scale together; letting players choose bigger risk for bigger payoff creates tension and excitement.
Sakurai: briefly pause (hit-stop/slow-mo) on big moments so players register and savor them.
Sakurai: alternate tension (squeeze) and release; relief after pressure is what makes peaks feel good.
Pacing: vary intensity like a wave - build-up, peak, rest - to avoid fatigue and boredom.
Keep players interested through pacing: introduce new mechanics/challenges regularly and give breathers between peaks.
Social mechanics are fun when players can cooperate, show off, and affect each other in meaningful but non-griefing ways.
Intrinsic rewards (mastery, curiosity, expression) outlast extrinsic ones; use extrinsic rewards to point at intrinsic fun.
Sid Meier: a game is a series of interesting decisions - trade-offs with no single obvious answer, made with enough information.
Psychology of fun: competence, autonomy, relatedness (self-determination theory), plus flow from balanced challenge.
A designer's counterintuitive secret to fun: constraints and friction, used well, create challenge and meaning.
Crash Course on gaming psychology: flow, rewards, learning curves, and why mastery feels good.
patterns: **Juice the most-repeated action most.** Squash/stretch, particles, sound layers, small screen shake, number pop-ups and hit-pause make simple actions satisfying.
**Feedback before content.** Several talks show the same mechanic going from dull to fun purely through feedback polish.
**Risk/reward and interesting decisions.** Let players choose bigger risk for bigger payoff; avoid single obvious best choices.
**Pacing in waves.** Alternate tension and release; introduce new mechanics regularly; stop for big moments.
**Randomness with care.** Use input randomness for variety; make output randomness feel fair (pity, visible odds).
**Intrinsic > extrinsic.** Mastery, curiosity, expression and social connection sustain fun; rewards should point at them, not replace them.
**Social moments.** Cooperation, showing off and friendly competition create memorable, shareable moments.
